one_liner: LevelDB/WiscKey-based LSM key-value store that swaps SSTable index search for per-file linear models; 1.23-1.78x faster lookups than WiscKey.
what_it_does: Bourbon is the OSDI'20 research LSM store. It is LevelDB 1.22 plus a WiscKey-style key-value separation: values go to an append-only vlog.txt and SSTables hold 12-byte (address, size) pointers. On top of that it adds learned indexes that locate keys inside SSTables. You use it through the normal leveldb::DB Open/Put/Get API, but the mode (MOD=7 Bourbon, 8 WiscKey, 0 plain LevelDB) and the tuning knobs are process-global variables in the adgMod namespace, not Options fields. This GitHub repo is a third-party snapshot of the authors' Bitbucket artifact. It adds CS736 course changes (a 'mode 9' that uses level models to find the file, and synchronous level learning, with no published numbers) and a 2023 PLR bug fix.
how_it_is_fast: Each SSTable gets a greedy piecewise linear regression model (GreedyPLR, adapted from RyanMarcus/plr) with error bound delta = 8. A lookup binary-searches the model's segments, predicts the key's position plus or minus delta, and reads only that byte range of the data block. Because entries are fixed-size, this replaces the index-block and data-block binary searches and also cuts the bytes loaded. A cost-benefit analyzer waits T_wait = 50 ms after a file is created, then learns the file only if the estimated lookup-time savings (per-level stats for positive and negative lookups) outweigh the training cost, so short-lived files under writes are skipped. The paper prefers file models to whole-level models because levels change constantly under writes; level learning only pays off when read-only.
when_to_use: Read-dominated LSM workloads where the working set is in the page cache or on Optane-class storage, so indexing dominates lookup time: about 1.6x on YCSB-C and 1.23-1.78x on in-memory read-only lookups vs WiscKey.

Fixed-width integer keys (zero-padded decimal strings such as the paper's 16 B keys) with smooth distributions. Fewer PLR segments means bigger gains: the linear dataset, at one segment per file, got 1.78x.
Point lookups and very short scans: 1.90x at range length 1 on the Amazon Reviews data, falling to 1.15x at 100 items.
Skewed (zipfian) reads on a memory-limited SATA-SSD machine where the hot set stays cached: 1.25x lower latency.
Reproducing or extending learned-index-in-LSM research. The repo ships the WiscKey baseline mode (-m 8), the read_cold driver and the scripts/run_*.sh experiment scripts.
when_not_to_use: Production storage. It is an abandoned research artifact configured through global variables. Value-log garbage collection was never ported (Vlog.h: 'Bourbon doesn't test on deletion'), so overwrites and deletes never reclaim space.
String or variable-length keys, or key compression. The paper says these are unsupported, and the code turns keys into integers by parsing ASCII decimal digits (SliceToInteger).

Write-heavy workloads. Writes are not sped up, and YCSB-A/F gain only 1.06-1.18x. Always re-learning at 50% writes did more total work than plain WiscKey, and level learning ran slower than baseline (0.87x).
Uniform random reads over data much larger than RAM on a SATA SSD. I/O dominates and the gain is only 1.04x.
If you need proof it beats RocksDB or stock LevelDB. The paper and repo compare only against their own WiscKey port, whatever the abstract's 'production LSMs' wording says.

integration.form: static lib (CMake target 'leveldb', a modified LevelDB 1.22; shared build via BUILD_SHARED_LIBS) plus the read_cold benchmark driver
integration.dependencies: Threads (required). snappy, crc32c and tcmalloc are auto-detected and optional. cxxopts is bundled (mod/cxxopts.hpp) for read_cold.
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 11), CMake >= 3.7. Compiler and version not documented.
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux in practice. mod/util.h includes <x86intrin.h> and uses __rdtscp, and the experiment scripts drop caches with sudo via /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches. Windows and non-x86 builds not documented.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. From reading the code: DBImpl's constructor sets the global pointer adgMod::db and the mode and key size are globals, so it is effectively one DB per process. DBImpl::Put appends to the VLog buffer before taking the DB mutex, and VLog has no lock. Get reads that buffer outside the mutex, so concurrent writers, or reads racing writes, look unsafe.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it keeps the leveldb::DB Open/Put/Get API, but the mode is set through globals, the on-disk format stores value-log pointers (not LevelDB-compatible), and in the code reviewed DB iterators never dereference the value log, so scans return raw 12-byte pointers rather than values.

gotchas: Wrong-result bug in the OSDI snapshot. If the same user key is written twice before a flush, both versions land in one SSTable, the PLR computes a NaN slope, and Get can fail. PR #7 (merged 2023-09-06) reported more than 3% bad Gets on a real-world trace. Only this fork's main branch has the fix (commit 0cd4715). The 'original bourbon' commit ad6abcb and the Bitbucket artifact (last updated 2020-10-05) predate it.

Fixed-size keys are assumed. generate_key zero-pads decimal keys to key_size, and block entry count and entry size are recorded once in globals, so the byte-range read assumes every entry has the same size.

Experiment config is fiddly. Mixed read-write runs need a rebuild with -DLEVEL_SWITCH=ON -DINTERNAL_TIMER_SWITCH=ON (CS736_README). The reported numbers use file models (--change_level_load, called 'Sazerac-File' in the README). The CPU frequency used to turn rdtscp cycles into time for the learning timers is hardcoded (reference_frequency = 2.6).

Hard to reproduce. Issue #6 reports segfaults in scripts/run_load_order.sh with no fix. The datasets are not published (issues #5, #8). The artifact's ready-made CloudLab machine was only for OSDI reviewers and UW-Madison students (issues #2, #3).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The catalogued learned indexes (PGM-index, RMI, RadixSpline, ALEX, LIPP) are in-memory structures over sorted arrays. Pick Bourbon only when you want learned indexing inside a persistent LSM store with write-aware re-learning, mainly as a research base. To embed an index, use PGM-index or ALEX. For a production LSM that measurably beats RocksDB, TerarkDB is the catalogued choice.
verified_claims_summary: The OSDI'20 paper ran 10M in-memory read-only lookups with 16 B integer keys and 64 B values on six datasets (four synthetic 64M-key sets, Amazon Reviews 33.5M, NY OSM 21.9M). Bourbon's file models (delta = 8) averaged about 2.65-3.64 us per lookup, 1.23-1.78x lower latency than WiscKey, the authors' LevelDB-derived key-value-separated LSM built from the same codebase. The machine was a 20-core Xeon E5-2660 with 160 GB RAM and a SATA SSD (an Optane SSD for the fast-storage runs); the compiler is not stated, and there is no RocksDB or stock-LevelDB head-to-head.
status_note: Abandoned: the fork's last commit is 2023-09-06 (a bug-fix PR) and the authors' Bitbucket original was last updated 2020-10-05; the code is BSD-3-Clause and about 5K LOC on top of a WiscKey port, fine for research but not production-ready (no value-log GC, global config).
